items.title: Inside the Iraqi Kurdish city caught between the US and Iran
items.content:
Inside the Iraqi Kurdish city caught between the US and Iran
Submitted by
Sean Mathews
on
Fri, 11/20/2026 - 19:37
Sulaymaniyah is reeling from the economic toll of the Iran war and grappling with an emboldened regional power next door
A market in the city of Sulaymaniyah in Iraq's Kurdistan Region is said to be the largest bazaar in the region, on 11 November 2026 (Sean Mathews/MEE)
Off
If
US
President Donald Trump has his way, Baran* will be out of business.
The thirty-year-old Kurd is a trader who buys diesel in Iraq and sells it in Afghanistan. It’s a stressful gig, but one that can generate a tidy profit in a place like Iraqi Kurdistan. A truck laden with $20,000 worth of diesel in Iraq can sell in Kabul for around $24,000, leaving around $2,000 for the trader once expenses are paid. But it has to make it through
Iran
first.
“The journey is more dangerous now. It’s harder to find drivers. The border isn’t as reliable. The price of diesel has also shot up,” Baran, whose name has been changed to protect his identity, told Middle East Eye.
Trump says instead of restarting strikes on Iran, he wants to choke its economy. In addition to a naval blockade, the US is pressing countries like
Turkey
,
Iraq
and
Pakistan
to seal their borders with Iran. Earlier this month, the US announced a task force to blockade trade across Iran’s land borders and the Caspian Sea.
Baran has no political beef with the US. On the contrary, he says, “George W. Bush overthrew Saddam Hussein. He helped Kurdistan. I don’t prefer Iran to the US,” he said over a glass of anise-flavoured Arak and hookahs at a restaurant in Sulaymaniyah.
“But this war has not been good for business or our economy.”
Baran is a microcosm of the city he calls home.
Sulaymaniyah
Nestled in the Zagros Mountains, Sulaymaniyah is Iraqi Kurdistan’s second largest city. Its beating heart is a sprawling bazaar where locals boast that any item a shopper desires can be procured. November is pomegranate season, and the fruit was plentiful. The label “Made In Iran” on packages and wrappings was also ubiquitous.
Sulaymaniyah prides itself on being more libertine than its rival Erbil. In the bazaar, more women go without a headscarf than with one.
“If people have $50 in their pockets, they will spend it to go out here,” Baran said. Bazaar merchants flick the city’s famed prayer beads, made of pistachio tree seeds, and tea boys run around keeping everyone well caffeinated.
On the surface, the vibrant bazaar gives an impression of prosperity, but the opposite is true.
“The price of food is unbearable for most people now. For some products, the increase is 200 percent,” Evin*, a 28-year-old shopper, complained to MEE. “We used to import so much from Iran, but now they aren’t exporting.”
Another young professional said they had to delay purchasing a new laptop computer because the price had shot up from $600 to $800 since the war started.
Because of taxes and logistics, Sulaymaniyah’s most competitive trade corridor to China runs through Iran. The region has a plethora of border posts that are more convenient than the Iraqi port of Basra - which feels a world away from here - or Turkey. Goods coming from the latter are also subject to higher taxes from Turkey and Erbil.
“In Iraqi Kurdistan, trade with Iran is a major part of the local economy,” Dlawer Ala’Aldeen, the president of the Middle East Research Institute, a Kurdish think-tank in Erbil, told MEE.
The US-Israeli war on Iran is taking a toll across the region. The economies of all the Arabian Gulf states are expected to shrink this year. Their pitches as tourism and business hubs are in jeopardy. This month alone, Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund headquarters and the tower housing state-oil company Aramco in Riyadh came under attack from the Houthis.
But Iraqi Kurdistan is a unique case.
'Living on a thin margin'
The region is convulsed by an internal political fissure that experts say could increase the sway of outside powers, particularly Turkey and Iran. This semiautonomous region of Iraq also lacks the deep pockets of Arab Gulf states to cushion geopolitical blows. The Kurdistan Regional Government (KRG) has been plagued by financial difficulties for years.
The region is supposed to receive around 15 percent of Iraq’s federal budget, more than 90 percent of which comes from oil revenue. Despite the war on Iran, Iraq exported more oil this month than at any time since 2019, but payments to the KRG are late.
Government employees are receiving their salaries months behind schedule. The rising costs of the Iran war have only compounded the pain.
Vehicles drive at the Iraq-Iran border crossing of Bashmagh near Sulaimaniyah in Iraq's autonomous Kurdistan region, on 11 March 2026 (AFP)
Iran has deep trade ties across Iraq and the Kurdistan Region. But Sulaymaniyah is particularly close to its eastern neighbour. The city was founded in 1784 under the Baban Emirate, which controlled parts of modern-day Iraq and Iran. Many founding Kurdish families hail from across the border.
“Slemani was already living on a thin margin,” Ala’Aldeen said, adding that the local economy depends on “cross-border trade, business, daily labour, and goods” from Iran.
“The war did not create that fragility; it exposed it: when Hormuz closed and when the United States pressed Iraq to close all but two crossings with Iran, Slemani felt it in prices and availability of goods,” he said. “Cutting Iran off will leave Slemani without many alternatives.”
Those trade ties are more interesting when one considers the pressure Iraq’s Kurdistan Region came under to join in the US-Israeli war on Iran earlier this year.
An estimated 40 million Kurds live between Syria, Iraq, Turkey and Iran. Although they never got a country when the Middle East was carved up by European colonial powers, Iraqi Kurdistan gained a high degree of autonomy in the 21st century because of the support it received from the US after the US invasion of Iraq.
For more than 20 years, Peshmerga fighters have been key American allies, most recently against the Islamic State militant group. The KRG also hosts some Iranian-Kurdish opposition groups who are backed by the US and Israel. When the Trump administration and Israel decided to attack Iran, they turned to Iraq’s Kurds to support opposition groups and fight across the border, but that plan never fully materialised.
'Impossible position to be in'
The KRG is dominated by two family dynasties, the Barzani family in Erbil, which leads the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP), and the Talabani family in Sulaymaniyah, which leads the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK).
In the 1990s, Iraq’s Kurds fought a civil war which saw the PUK receive support from Iran, and the KDP from Turkey. Because of its geography and economy, Sulaymaniyah continues to be viewed as closer to Iran, so much so that Bafel Talabani, the PUK leader, denied a reporter's question at a conference earlier this month in Sulaymaniyah, put to him that he was in Iran’s “pocket”.
In reality, both the PUK and KDP are closely aligned with the US.
Female members of the Iranian Kurdish opposition Komala party carry the body of a Peshmerga fighter in the autonomous Kurdistan region, on 16 April 2026 (AFP)
Among American officials,
Bafel Talabani
is known to enjoy hanging out with former American Joint Special Operations Command fighters, better known as “JSOC guys”. His brother, Qubad, the deputy prime minister of Iraqi Kurdistan, is married to a former State Department official.
A former US intelligence official told MEE that the PUK was actually seen by members of the Trump administration as more receptive to plans to support Kurdish opposition groups in Iran because it was lobbying for greater attention in Washington. The PUK's territory in the KRG also shares a longer border with Iran.
The PUK was courting the Trump administration in part over frustration that its rival, the KDP, had greater access in Washington as a result of controlling the Kurdistan region’s presidency.
The tensions between the two parties have erupted into a major political rift that experts say risks splitting the KRG. Talabani withdrew the PUK from the region's parliament in November and told a forum in Sulaymaniyah that the KRG was already living “the reality of two governments and two administrations”.
In the end, neither the PUK nor KDP joined the US war effort. A decision that many Kurds welcomed.
"Kurdistan was right to refuse to be embroiled in this war. A collapse in Tehran would not arrive as a clean handover. It would arrive as chaos on Kurdistan's longest border: refugees, armed factions, a power vacuum, and a fight over who controls Iranian Kurdistan," Ala’Aldeen at the  Middle East Research Institute, told MEE.
Internal politics are at play now, too.
Bafel Talabani is courting members of Baghdad’s ruling Shia Coordination Framework for an upper hand against the KDP. The Shia Coordination Framework is aligned with Tehran.
The Kurdistan Region is also militarily exposed. It lacks proper air defence systems. The last US troops left Erbil, the region's capital, in September, completing a full US withdrawal from Iraq. The region faced hundreds of Iranian missile and drone strikes
during the war.
“Bafel Talabani is an ambitious guy. He speaks with everyone, too. He’s pragmatic. But he faces a very difficult position. He is seeking US support, but Iran sees Sulaymaniyah as its backyard. It’s an impossible position to be in,” Oral Toga, a senior researcher at the Centre for Iranian Studies in Ankara, told MEE.
'Iran has the upper hand'
At a strategic forum hosted in Sulaymaniyah earlier this month, PUK officials emphasised their desire for dialogue and partnership with Iran. Bafel Talabani himself
said
that Iran had emerged “stronger but different” from the US-Israeli war and criticised those who characterise the country as being run by “mad mullahs”.
Recounting a recent trip he made to Iran, he offered a very different assessment to that proposed by members of the Trump administration who have characterised Iran as on the verge of economic collapse.
"I thought I was in London," Talabani said, noting that "less than 50 percent of ladies and girls had scarves" and that restaurants were filled with young people dancing.
This overview shows Iraq's northeastern city of Sulaymaniyah in the autonomous Kurdistan region at sunset, on 18 October 2024 (AFP)
Tehran is now pressuring Iraqi Kurdistan to clamp down on Kurdish opposition groups. In a meeting in September with Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, Bafal Talabani promised not to allow Iraqi Kurdistan to become "a haven for harming or threatening" the Islamic Republic.
"As an ally of Mr Trump and, strangely, an ally of the Iranians [I say] the mighty US can [talk to Iran],” he said at the forum.
“The region feels Iran has a strategic upper hand at the moment. It’s not just Iraqi Kurdistan, but the Gulf states too. They all want to avoid Iran’s wrath," Sarhang Hamasaeed, an independent Middle East analyst, told MEE.
“But Iran has shown that in this fight it isn’t factoring those relations in. Iraq has been the economic lungs of Iran, but Iran didn’t spare their exports through Hormuz," he added.
Given its land border with Iran, Sulaymaniyah is even more vulnerable to reprisals should the war resume.
"The Kurds in Iraq were Iran's target practice in prior years, well before Iran's war with the US and Israel. They know, and don't want to be on the receiving end of Iranian strikes," Hamasaeed said.
“Between the US and Iran, they have to appease Iran more, because Trump won’t strike them with drones and missiles  - Iran will,” he said.
The US will not fire missiles at Iraqi Kurdistan like Iran, but America's foreign policy could endanger the region.
Many in Sulaymaniyah believe the US will not be content until it collapses the Iranian government.
Trump himself said as much on a radio show this month. When asked by a radio host whether he would consider it a “defeat” for him if the Islamic Republic was still in power at the end of his term, Trump said “absolutely”.
"The worst thing for Sulaymaniyah and Iraqi Kurdistan would be a failed state across the border. We need stability," a Kurdish official in the city told MEE.

items.title: US sanctions Iranian 'oil trustees' it accuses of evading sanctions
items.content:
US sanctions Iranian 'oil trustees' it accuses of evading sanctions
The US Treasury on Friday imposed sanctions on four Iranians who served as "oil trustees".
It said they had sought to collect funds from illicit international oil sales and pass them to the Iranian government to evade earlier sanctions and a US naval blockade.
In many cases, the trustees kept the oil revenues for personal gain, the Treasury said in a statement.
Those sanctioned include Mohammad Javad Bavand, a former intelligence officer in Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, and Majid Taj, brother of Mehdi Taj, the president of Iran’s football federation.

items.title: Palestinian man killed near Ramallah as Israeli raids sweep occupied West Bank
items.content:
Palestinian man killed near Ramallah as Israeli raids sweep occupied West Bank
A Palestinian man was killed by Israeli forces near Ramallah on Friday as the forces carried out raids, detentions and a home demolition across the occupied West Bank, the Palestinian news agency Wafa reported.
Hamza Masoud Salim Abdo, 42, was killed in Dura al-Qare, northeast of Ramallah, by Israeli forces who are still withholding his body, the Palestinian General Authority of Civil Affairs said.
In Jaba, south of Jenin, Israeli forces beat a man who was taken to hospital, the Palestinian Red Crescent said. A convoy of army vehicles later stormed the town and detained two young men. In nearby Qabatiya, soldiers fired on a vehicle and detained two people.
In Jericho, a young Palestinian man was shot in the foot during a raid on the al-Bayader neighbourhood.
South of Hebron, Israeli forces raided al-Fawwar refugee camp as residents left Friday prayers, firing tear gas and beating a young man who was later hospitalised.
In nearby Beit Ummar, Israeli forces stormed the town, ordered merchants to close their shops and fired barrages of tear gas and stun grenades, according to local media activist Mohammad Awad. He said soldiers severely beat and detained two men, aged 22 and 45.
In the Tulkarm governorate, several young men were detained as Israeli forces raided the town of Anabta.
Also on Friday, Israeli bulldozers demolished a home in al-Mazra’a al-Gharbiya, northwest of Ramallah.
Meanwhile, Israeli settlers stole the contents of a roadside fruit stand south of Jenin and trees from a nursery in Jaba, surveillance footage showed.
Israeli soldiers block a road, preventing access to Palestinian-owned olive groves during harvest season, in Abu Falah near Ramallah, occupied West Bank, on 20 November 2026 (Reuters/Ammar Awad)

items.title: US Vice President Vance declines to say he would have ordered Iran strikes
items.content:
By Bo Erickson and Jacob Bogage
WASHINGTON, Nov 20 (Reuters) - US Vice President JD Vance on Friday declined to say whether he would have authorized strikes on Iran to prevent the country from developing a nuclear weapon, sidestepping President Donald Trump's calls for him to say the attacks were necessary and that he would carry them out again.
Speaking at a White House press conference alongside Trump, Vance said the decision to attack Iran in February was Trump's call, "and my job is to support the president of the United States."

items.title: US right-wing voices attack Islam online after a study projects global Muslim majority by 2035
items.content:
US right-wing voices attack Islam online after a study projects global Muslim majority by 2035
Submitted by
Nouran Saleh
on
Fri, 11/20/2026 - 19:32
Pew Research study projects Islam to grow by 80 percent worldwide by 2070, to the ire of the US right wing
Muslim pilgrims perform Umrah around the Kaaba, Islam's holiest shrine, in Saudi Arabia's holy city of Mecca, on 20 October 2026 (AFP)
Off
A new
study
by Pew Research Center has become a trigger for Islamophobic attacks from many online after it projected that Muslims will outnumber Christians by 2035.
The study on the future of world religions between 2020 and 2070 projects that Muslims will grow to 3.6 billion worldwide by 2070, growing by 80 percent, prompted by their dual demographic of youth and high fertility.
The study also showcases that Pakistan will surpass Indonesia as the country with the most Muslims by 2070.
In North America, Muslims will more than triple in number, with migration playing a big role, growing by nine million in the US, but will still make up only four percent of the country’s total population. Currently, Muslims only make up 1-1.6 percent of the total US population.
Right-wing commentators and politicians immediately took to social media to express their “concern” over the study’s projections, despite the report stating that Muslims would make up only a small percentage of the US population.
Texas House Representative Keith Self spotlighted immigration, claiming that it had failed the US.
“Our nation is founded on the Christian faith. If we don’t get a handle on this, we are going to lose our country, our freedoms, and our heritage,” he wrote on X.
Unfettered mass immigration has failed America.
Our nation is founded on the Christian faith. If we don’t get a handle on this, we are going to lose our country, our freedoms, and our heritage.
We cannot become the UK or France. A house divided cannot stand!
https://t.co/CODOxx9NNW
— Rep. Keith Self (@RepKeithSelf)
November 19, 2026
Former White House press secretary, Karoline Leavitt, joined the freight train, urging Americans to "have more babies".
Get married, have more babies, raise them in the church, and teach them to love America.
pic.twitter.com/Zs96P8Jfd9
— Karoline Leavitt (@karolineleavitt)
November 19, 2026
Turning Point USA also released a statement regarding the study, warning Americans to "wake up".
Islam is projected to become the world’s largest religion by 2035, according to new data from Pew Research Center.
The clock is ticking, America. Wake up.
— Turning Point USA (@TPUSA)
November 18, 2026
The Conservative nonprofit, Centre for Renewing America, also commented on the Islamophobic remarks by posting on X: "We need to take the work of preserving our nation VERY seriously, and part of that is defeating Islam in America.”
We need to take the work of preserving our nation VERY seriously and part of that is defeating Islam in America. We have a history, a culture, and an inheritance worth preserving and we can't afford to be complacent about threats to them.
https://t.co/PaPRJy7j9G
— Center for Renewing America (@amrenewctr)
November 19, 2026
These racist remarks are not new and follow a pattern of increased anti-Muslim sentiment in the US. Most recently, New York City Mayor
Zohran Mamdani
has been targeted with racist comments about his moustache, with some comparing him to the deceased dictator of Iraq, Saddam Hussein, and calling him a terrorist.
Despite an increase in anti-Muslim sentiment, a
record
number of hijabis and Muslims were
elected
to public office during the midterm elections in the US this month.
The Pew study projected a 29 percent increase in the world's population and added that only Muslims and Christians would keep pace with that growth rate. It also said that the US will no longer have a Christian majority by 2070, but Christians will still remain the largest religious group in the country.

items.title: Trump cites good talks with Putin on Ukraine, holds back on security guarantees
items.content:
By Bo Erickson and Doina Chiacu
WASHINGTON, Nov 20 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump said on Friday that he and Russian leader Vladimir Putin held very good talks on Ukraine during their meeting in China, but added he didn't want to discuss security guarantees for Ukraine without a broader peace deal.
"We're having very good talks. I think there's a real good chance that we can get it done," Trump said at a White House press conference after his trip to Asia, where he met Putin and Chinese President XiJinping.

items.title: Yemen's Houthis launch strikes after Saudi coalition's 'special operation'
items.content:
Yemen's Houthis launched strikes on the Saudi capital Riyadh on Saturday, after vowing reprisals for a "special operation" by the Saudi-led coalition fighting them.
Saudi Arabia has been battling a surge in attacks since fighting reignited in neighbouring Yemen's civil war this summer, where Riyadh backs the internationally recognised government against the Houthis.
An AFP journalist reported hearing two explosions shortly after authorities issued an alert, later lifted, saying the city was "under a hostile aerial threat".

items.title: Trump envoys met Qatari officials in Berlin to discuss US-Iran mediation, report says
items.content:
Trump envoys met Qatari officials in Berlin to discuss US-Iran mediation, report says
US
President Donald Trump’s envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner met senior
Qatari
officials in Berlin on Thursday to discuss mediation efforts between the US and
Iran
, Axios
reported
on Friday, citing two sources with knowledge of the meeting.
The meeting came as Qatar’s Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani was in
Germany
on a visit.
Following talks with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz in Berlin, the emir called for diplomatic efforts to de-escalate conflicts across the Middle East.
On the sidelines of the visit, Qatari Foreign Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani met his German counterpart Johann Wadephul.
The two discussed ongoing diplomatic efforts and joint coordination to de-escalate tensions and enhance security and stability in the region, according to the Qatari foreign ministry.

items.title: Trump says US will find out about Iranian dirty bomb plot 'rumour'
items.content:
Trump says US will find out about Iranian dirty bomb plot 'rumour'
US President Donald Trump said on Friday that there was a "rumour" that Iran was building a dirty bomb. He added that if Iran was doing so, the United States would find out and stop it.
CNN had
reported
earlier this week that US intelligence indicated Iran could be attempting to build a dirty bomb and detonate it in Washington.
Iran's foreign ministry denied the allegations on Tuesday, calling them "baseless".
A dirty bomb is far less destructive than a nuclear bomb, which relies on a fission reaction.
Speaking to reporters, Trump also repeated his claim that the US has "total control" over the Strait of Hormuz.
"Last week, we took out record amounts of oil from the Hormuz Strait. Our navy has a blockade," he said. "We have total control over the Hormuz Strait."
"Iran will never have a nuclear weapon, ever," he added.
US President Donald Trump points as reporters raise their hands to ask questions during a press conference at the White House in Washington, DC, 20 November 2026 (REUTERS/Kylie Cooper)

items.title: Houthi attacks add to worries over Trump Saudi nuclear power pact
items.content:
By Patricia Zengerle and Timothy Gardner
Nov 20 (Reuters) - Houthi attacks on Saudi infrastructure are adding to concerns about US President Donald Trump's proposed nuclear power pact with the kingdom, weeks before US senators are due to vote on whether to block the agreement.
Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis have intensified drone and missile strikes on Saudi airports, oil facilities and office buildings, raising questions about Riyadh's ability to secure nuclear plants that would be built under the pact.

Chambers’s case is the
first known instance
of the US seeking to extradite a citizen over alleged support for Hamas, an accusation apparently tied to an international money-laundering charge in the criminal complaint underpinning the extradition request and donations to organizations helping Palestinians in Gaza.

items.title: نفذت قواتنا المسلحة بعون الله عملية عسكرية نوعية استهدفت محطة الشقيق الكهربائية وميناء جيزان وكانت الإصابات دقيقة ومباشرة وخلفت أضرارًا…
items.content:
نفذت قواتنا المسلحة بعون الله عملية عسكرية نوعية استهدفت محطة الشقيق الكهربائية وميناء جيزان وكانت الإصابات دقيقة ومباشرة وخلفت أضرارًا كبيرة.
يأتي هذا الاستهداف ردا على استهداف العدو السعودي المجرم لمحطات كهرباء صعدة والمخا، واستهداف سابق ظهر اليوم لأحد الأرصفة في ميناء الحديدة.
نؤكد للعدو السعودي أن أي استهداف لميناء الحديدة أو محطات الكهرباء سيتم الرد عليها مباشرة في موانئه ومحطاته الكهربائية.

items.title: Saudi-led forces strike Yemen port as Houthis warn airlines off the kingdom
items.content:
By Yasmine Ghania and Muhammad Al Gebaly
Nov 20 (Reuters) - The Saudi-led coalition fighting Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis said it had struck the Red Sea port of Hodeidah to destroy Houthi capabilities on Friday, as the militants warned airlines to avoid Saudi airspace, pledging new air strikes within hours.
The developments, a day after the group struck the tallest skyscraper in Riyadh, signalled a worsening of a conflict that has brought a humanitarian crisis to Yemen and severe disruption to Saudi Arabia, in parallel with the US-led war against Iran.

items.title: In Yemen's Aden, divided government forces prepare for a Houthi assault
items.content:
ADEN, Nov 20 (Reuters) - As Yemen's Houthis push closer towards the temporary capital Aden against fragmented government forces, the city's inhabitants face a bleak choice: stay under fire or leave for an impoverished countryside.
Aden has had no major warfare since bitter street battles of 2015, soon after the internationally recognised government fled Houthi-run Sanaa and made the port city its base, but it is now being hit by missile and drone strikes.

items.title: Myanmar genocide judgment may bolster Gaza case against Israel
items.content:
By Anthony Deutsch and Stephanie van den Berg
THE HAGUE, Nov 20 (Reuters) - The International Court of Justice's landmark ruling that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya will strengthen South Africa's genocide case against Israel over the war in Gaza, legal experts said, establishing a precedent that genocidal intent can coexist with a military objective.
While the conflicts in Gaza and Myanmar are legally distinct, both cases before theWorld Court are based on allegations that states breached their obligations under the 1948 Genocide Convention.

items.title: Former French PM de Villepin launches 2027 presidential bid
items.content:
By Michel Rose and Elizabeth Pineau
PARIS, Nov 20 (Reuters) - Former French prime minister Dominique de Villepin announced on Friday that he would run for president in the 2027 election, joining an increasingly crowded field of centrist and centre-right candidates seeking to succeed Emmanuel Macron.
De Villepin, 73, who launched his own political movement last year, said he was running to heal a divided and "rotten" France, attacking what he called the "dead star" ofMacron's movementwhile rejecting both the far right and the far left.

items.title: US reacts cautiously to Myanmar genocide ruling as EU praises ‘critical’ role of UN’s top court
items.content:
Reactions to ICJ ruling underline global divisions over court with China raising concerns about judicial overreach
The US has greeted with caution the world’s highest court’s ruling that
Myanmar committed genocide
against its Rohingya minority, while China has raised concerns of judicial overreach.
Reactions to Thursday’s historic ruling underlined deep international division over the role of the court and similar institutions. The international court of justice (ICJ) had never previously found a state responsible for genocide and the decision could set a precedent for future genocide claims, notably a
case against Israel
.

items.content:
بورما تصف قرار إدانتها بإبادة الروهينغا بأنه "غير عادل" والصين تقول إنه لا "يساهم في حل الأزمة"
وصفت المتحدثة باسم الرئاسة في بورما، الجمعة، قرار محكمة العدل الدولية الذي أدان بلادها بارتكاب إبادة جماعية ضد أقلية الروهينغا بأنه "ليس عادلا". ونفت بورما مرارا أن تكون ارتكبت إبادة، مشيرة إلى أن قواتها استهدفت "انتفاضة مسلحة". من جهة أخرى أبدت الصين تحفظها تجاه القرار وحذرت من تجاوز القضاء الدولي لصلاحياته، معتبرة أن هذه الخطوات "لا تساهم" في حل الأزمة.

items.title: ‘Weak and dizzy’: the secretive ICE force-feeding tactics that ended a Cuban father’s hunger strike
items.content:
Exclusive: Luis Alejandro Cora Pérez says in messages to Guardian from inside Texas facility pain of force-feeding caused him to break strike
The text message that came from inside the Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention center was stark: “I have spent five days eating regular food. If I don’t eat it, they put the tube in me to feed me.”
A Cuban asylum seeker, Luis Alejandro Cora Pérez, 32, said in messages to the Guardian this month that he was still weak and dizzy after three months without eating, but that he had broken his hunger strike because being force-fed was just too painful.

items.title: العراق: قوات الأمن تنتشر في معقل "كتائب حزب الله" لتنفيذ اتفاق تسوية يهدف إلى خفض التوتر
items.content:
العراق: قوات الأمن تنتشر في معقل "كتائب حزب الله" لتنفيذ اتفاق تسوية يهدف إلى خفض التوتر
قال مسؤولو أمن عراقيون، في مؤتمر صحفي، الجمعة، إن قوات الأمن العراقية بدأت الانتشار في منطقة جرف الصخر، معقل "كتائب حزب الله" المسلحة، وذلك في إطار اتفاق تسوية يهدف إلى تخفيف التوتر مع أقوى فصيل مسلح حليف لإيران في البلاد. وفي خطوة بالغة الخطورة، أمر رئيس الوزراء علي الزيدي في وقت سابق من الأسبوع قوات الأمن بالاستعداد للتحرك ضد "كتائب حزب الله"، التي اتهمها المسؤولون بإدارة شبكة لتهريب النفط، قالت السلطات إنها هرّبت كميات من الخام المملوك للدولة تُقدّر قيمتها بمئات الملايين من الدولارات.

items.title: California’s coastal communities on alert as biggest waves in years hit state
items.content:
Hazard warnings issued throughout week after powerful swells and waves of more than 9 metres recorded
Multiple coastal hazard warnings were issued this week across California as successive areas of low pressure generated powerful swells and large breaking waves for coastal communities. Beaches and piers were closed last weekend as large waves crashed into California’s coastline. Offshore National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration buoys recorded wave heights of greater than 30ft (9 metres) last Friday. The Monterey, California, buoy recorded a wave height of 34.1ft, which would make it the highest reading in 30 years.
Coastal warnings extended from last weekend through this week, with alerts extending until Friday night. Waves of 10-18ft are expected, with local sets of 18-22ft for San Luis Obispo county beaches and Santa Barbara county central coast beaches. These Pacific storm systems are also bringing unsettled conditions across the western US, with heavy rain, mountain snow, and strong winds through the coming days. Already, record-breaking rainfall affected San Fransisco on Wednesday, with heavy rain also causing 32,000 customers to lose power in Sacramento. Into this weekend, a further area of low pressure will bring considerable amounts of moisture for southern Oregon and northern California. By Sunday night, more than 100mm (4in) of rain is expected in places, with further snowfall for areas such as Donner Pass across the northern Sierra Nevada mountains.

items.content:

اعتبرت قاضية أمريكية في ولاية فلوريدا، الخميس، أن توماس ماركل، والد دوقة ساسكس البريطانية ميغان ماركل، يتمتع بالأهلية الذهنية الكافية لمواجهة التهمة، في قضية حيازة صور اعتداء جنسي على أطفال. وجاء قرار القاضية ليندسي جريفين مصادقا على تقييم طبيبة نفسية منتدبة من المحكمة، أكدت قدرة ماركل البالغ من العمر 82 عاما على استيعاب مسار المحاكمة والمشاركة بفعالية في الدفاع عن نفسه، وذلك عقب توجيه التهمة الجنائية إليه رسميا في الخامس من نوفمبر/تشرين الثاني الجاري.

items.content:
تايوان تطلع "ميتا" على رصد شبكة رقمية يشتبه في ارتباطها بحملة تأثير صينية تستهدف الانتخابات
أبلغت السلطات في تايوان شركة "ميتا" أنها رصدت شبكة رقمية تضم نحو 2700 حساب على منصة "ثريدز" التابعة لها، يُشتبه في ارتباطها بحملة حرب إعلامية صينية منسقة للتأثير على الانتخابات. وتُظهر بيانات داخلية ومصادر حكومية  أن غالبية هذه الحسابات جرى إنشاؤها على دفعات خلال الأشهر الأربعة الماضية، وتبين أن معظمها صينية. في المقابل أكد متحدث باسم شركة "ميتا"، التي تمتلك أيضا منصتي فيسبوك وإنستاغرام، أن الشركة حذفت الحسابات التي أبلغت عنها حكومة تايوان.

كشف مصدر مقرّب من البيت الأبيض، الخميس، إقالة مسؤول الأمن السيبراني شون كيرنكروس، بدعم من الرئيس دونالد ترامب، وذلك على وقع موجة أعطال تقنية غير مسبوقة طالت حركة السفر وخدمات الاتصالات والتجارة الإلكترونية، وعطلت شبكة اتصالات داخلية سرية للغاية تابعة لوكالة الأمن القومي. ووفق مصدر مقرّب من البيت الأبيض، استند قرار الإقالة إلى عدم ملاءمة كيرنكروس للمنصب، ليتجه الخيار مؤقتا نحو تعيين كيرستين ديفيز، رئيسة قسم المعلومات في وزارة الدفاع والحاصلة على موافقة مجلس الشيوخ.

items.title: Race to be next UN secretary general exposes divisions among world powers
items.content:
Debate about dominance of permanent five members could reignite if major powers block Costa Rican frontrunner
The race to become the next UN secretary general could reach a decisive moment on Friday when a UN security council vote is likely to reveal whether the Costa Rican frontrunner for the post would be blocked by the big powers. If so, the setback will reignite a debate about the dominance of the permanent five (P5) members at the United Nations.
Rebeca Grynspan, an economist and UN insider who is from a family of Polish-Jewish wartime refugees to Costa Rica, has been in the lead in all but one of the eight straw polls of the 15 UN security council members since the first secret ballot was held on 30 July. Each member goes down the list of candidates, casting an “encourage”, “discourage” or “no opinion” vote for each candidate.

items.title: Iraq university’s removal of male professors teaching women sparks weeks of protests
items.content:
Al-Qadisiyah University’s move a sign of the country’s slide into a Taliban-like gender segregation, say activists
The removal of male professors teaching female students at a university in southern Iraq has sparked protests and been criticised by activists as a Taliban-like gender segregation policy.
As many as 400 women are estimated to have joined protests over the past two weeks calling for the return of their professors at Al-Qadisiyah University in a move that appears to have surprised its administrators.

items.title: العراق: تسوية تتيح انتشار القوات الحكومية في جرف الصخر وسط خلاف بشأن انسحاب كتائب حزب الله
items.content:

تستعد القوات العراقية للانتشار الجمعة في منطقة جرف الصخر، معقل كتائب حزب الله المقربة من إيران، بعد التوصل إلى تسوية لتجنب مواجهة بين الحكومة والفصيل المسلح. وجاء الاتفاق إثر تدخل قائد فيلق القدس الإيراني إسماعيل قاآني، في ظل توتر أثارته اتهامات للكتائب بتهريب النفط. لكن مصير قوات الفصيل في المنطقة لا يزال غير محسوم، رغم إعلان مسؤول عراقي أنها ستنتقل إلى مواقع أخرى.

items.title: تصاعد الهجمات الحوثية على السعودية وترامب يؤجل البت في ضربات جديدة على إيران
items.content:
تصاعد الهجمات الحوثية على السعودية وترامب يؤجل البت في ضربات جديدة على إيران
أعلنت السعودية تعرض برج في مركز الملك عبدالله المالي بالرياض لهجوم حوثي ألحق أضرارا مادية بعدة طوابق. وأعلنت جماعة الحوثي استهداف مطار الملك خالد الدولي في العاصمة وقاعدة خميس مشيط الجوية، في حين أفاد إعلام تابع لها بشن غارات سعودية على صنعاء. من جهته، قال الرئيس الأمريكي دونالد ترامب الخميس إنه سيؤجل اتخاذ قرار بشأن شن هجمات جديدة على إيران إلى ما بعد مطلع عام 2027. وفي مضيق هرمز، أعلن الحرس الثوري الإيراني انفجار ناقلتي نفط إثر اصطدامهما بألغام بحرية، فيما تواصل الولايات المتحدة وثلاث دول أوروبية الضغط على طهران للسماح باستئناف عمليات التفتيش في منشآتها النووية.

👈 اقرأ المزيد: https://f24.my/CIO8.g

المفوضية الأوروبية تؤكد تعرضها لهجوم إلكتروني باستخدام الذكاء الاصطناعي وتفتح تحقيقا
كشفت المفوضية الأوروبية الخميس عن تعرض أنظمتها لهجوم إلكتروني باستخدام أدوات الذكاء الاصطناعي، رُصد في 22 أكتوبر/تشرين الأول، ما دفعها إلى تعطيل عدد من تطبيقاتها مؤقتا. وأكدت أن التحقيقات لا تزال جارية لتحديد حجم الهجوم، مشيرة إلى عدم وجود أدلة على تسرب بيانات موظفيها.

👈 اقرأ المزيد: https://f24.my/CILw.g

items.title: في صراعها مع الحوثيين.. الحكومة اليمنية أمام تحد الحفاظ على شرعيتها
items.content: التطورات الميدانية الأخيرة تشير إلى أن التحالف العسكري السعودي يواجه أزمة في اليمن. ففي الوقت الذي يتقدم فيه الحوثيون يتفكك تحالف خصومهم. كما أن أمن أحد الطرق التجارية العالمية المهمة أصبح على المحك.
